analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to open the Arctic refuge's 1.5-million-acre coastal plain to oil leasing drew 34 sponsors, including 3 Democrats, but died in committee after a single April 2000 hearing and never got a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill repeals the 1980 ban on oil and gas leasing in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain and orders the Interior Department to hold competitive lease sales, with the first sale within 20 months. It declares drilling there 'compatible' with the refuge's purpose by law, deems a 1987 environmental review adequate, and bars the Interior Secretary from closing any other areas to drilling. Revenue from leases would go to the Treasury, with a fixed share paid to Alaska.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain access to leases on roughly 1.5 million acres of the refuge's coastal plain that have been off-limits since 1980, with mandatory lease sales of at least 200,000 acres and rights-of-way for pipelines across the plain. Alaska receives a fixed share of federal leasing and royalty revenue. Two Alaska Native corporations, Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, receive title conveyances to lands within the coastal plain, and leaseholders are encouraged to hire Alaska Natives.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the statutory prohibition on oil and gas leasing in the coastal plain and directs the Interior Department to establish a competitive leasing program there.

Mandates a first lease sale of 200,000 to 300,000 acres within 20 months of enactment, with further sales at least every two years, giving companies a firm schedule rather than a discretionary process.

Directs the Secretary to grant rights-of-way and easements across the coastal plain for oil and gas transportation, and to convey surface lands to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and subsurface rights to Arctic Slope Regional Corporation.
Deposits all lease revenues in the Treasury, with a fixed semiannual percentage paid to the State of Alaska.

Includes guardrails: leases require at least a 12.5% royalty, fair market value for the public, antitrust review of bids, reclamation bonding, and a requirement to use the best commercially available technology.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the environmental cost: drilling would permanently change a protected Arctic wilderness, and the bill limits the government's ability to say no. It lets Congress, not biologists, declare drilling 'compatible' with the refuge's purpose, deems a 1987 environmental review sufficient without update, caps protected Special Areas at 45,000 acres out of 1.5 million, and takes away the Interior Secretary's authority to close any other lands to drilling. Challenges to agency rules go straight to the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals on a 90-day deadline.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the section of the Alaska National Interest Lands Conservation Act that has barred drilling in the coastal plain since 1980, ending that protection permanently rather than through case-by-case review.

Congress itself declares drilling compatible with the refuge's purpose and deems the 1987 Final Legislative Environmental Impact Statement adequate for all lease sales and rights-of-way, removing the ordinary environmental review process for these decisions.

The Interior Secretary's only authority to close land to drilling is the 45,000-acre Special Areas provision, and judicial review of drilling rules is channeled exclusively to the D.C. Circuit on a 90-day filing deadline, narrowing the ways the public can contest decisions.

Environmental conditions in the bill depend on regulations the Interior Department would write later; a future administration could write weaker rules, and the bill's declaration that no further environmental findings are required limits the legal check on that.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill promises domestic oil supply, federal revenue shared with Alaska, and jobs, with real protections on paper: a 12.5% royalty floor, bonding, antitrust review, and seasonal closures to protect caribou calving. But its design undercuts those protections. By legislating the environmental conclusion in advance, freezing the 1987 review as adequate, and capping protected acreage at 3% of the coastal plain while stripping the Secretary of any other closure authority, the bill trades permanent development of a unique wilderness for revenue and supply that could also be pursued elsewhere. The environmental risk falls on the refuge and the communities that depend on its caribou and fish.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2000, sent to the Senate Energy Committee, which held one hearing in April, and then sat there until the Congress ended in January 2001 without a committee vote or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Murkowski introduced S. 2214 on March 8, 2000 with 33 original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The committee held a hearing on April 5, 2000 (printed as S.Hrg. 106-605), but no further action was taken on the bill for the rest of the 106th Congress.
The 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001, so the bill died in committee without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the Arctic refuge's coastal plain stayed legally closed to drilling. Conservation interests and Alaska Native communities that depend on the refuge's caribou and wildlife were better off; oil companies gained no access, and the Treasury and Alaska gained no new leasing revenue.

for.name: Sen. Frank Murkowski
for.role: U.S. Senator from Alaska and Chairman, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it to his own committee, which held a hearing in April 2000 but never marked it up or reported it.

for.name: 30 of 55 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors of the drilling bill.

for.name: 3 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors (Sens. Akaka, Breaux, and Inouye).

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Opposed drilling in the Arctic refuge; his administration's opposition made Senate action on such a bill unlikely, and he had previously vetoed 1995 legislation containing an ANWAR drilling provision.

against.name: Conservation and environmental groups
against.role: National environmental organizations, including groups focused on the Arctic refuge
against.what_they_did: Campaigns against opening the refuge to drilling, keeping the issue visible and politically costly for senators.

sides.party_line_note: Of the bill's 34 original sponsors, 30 were Republicans and 3 were Democrats (Akaka, Breaux, Inouye); no floor vote ever occurred to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill opens 1.5 million acres of the refuge coastal plain to mandatory competitive leasing with rights-of-way for transport, a prize oil companies had sought since 1980. Its gain comes at the cost of a protected public wilderness, though the public also receives royalties and revenue from any leases.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations (Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation)
industries.note: The bill conveys the surface estate to Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and the subsurface estate beneath it to Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, and directs leaseholders to give a fair share of jobs and contracts to Alaska Natives. Some Alaska Native communities support drilling revenue, while Gwich'in communities that rely on the caribou herd oppose development.

industries.industry: Oil field services and pipeline transportation
industries.note: New exploration, production, and mandated rights-of-way across the coastal plain would generate construction and transport work tied to moving oil from the refuge, serving the industry's needs on protected public land.

Alaska would receive a fixed semiannual share of all federal leasing revenue, adding to a state budget already built on oil. That revenue would come from developing a federal refuge rather than from any new tax on residents.
